This guideline addresses multifactorial management programs first, and then reviews each category of intervention within the physical therapy scope of practice The results of individual systematic reviews are summarized in the accompanying tables, and the risk ratio, rate ratio, and 95% confidence intervals are provided. Risk ratio refers to the proportion in the number of people falling in the intervention group compared to a comparison group, and the rate ratio refers to the proportion in the number of fall events in the intervention group compared to a comparison group. For both measures, a number less than one indicates a decreased risk and greater than 1 indicates an increased risk. The 95% confidence interval indicates the statistical significance of estimated risk or rate ratio. If the 95% confidence interval contains the value of 1.0, then the estimate of the risk ratio or rate ratio indicates no statistically significant difference between the control group and the intervention group. Screening Physical therapists’ management of falls is predicated on their ability to identify fall risk and movement dysfunction as part of a multifactorial evaluation process to guide treatment choice. In 2017, through the Geriatrics Evidence Database to Guide Effectiveness Initiative (GeriEDGE) task force, Lusardi et al published a systematic review of history questions, self-report measures, and performance-based measures for assessing fall risk of community-dwelling older adults.13 This CPG developed a screening process using these results13 and the previous guidance statement recommendations.12 The screening process includes medical history questions, self-report measures, and performancebased functional measures as part of a multifactorial falls screening13 (see Table 3). The GDG did not systematically review the evidence for screening for falls risk, thus we indicate the level of evidence for screening, but do not provide specific recommendations for falls risk screening. The medical history questions, self-report measures, and performance-based measures with the highest post-test probability of identifying falls risk align with the Center for Disease Control (CDC) “Stopping Elderly Accidents, Death, and Injuries” (STEADI) processes20 and recent guidelines on the management of falls.15 The details are provided in the Falls Management Algorithm (Figure 1). Screening may include self-report measures of falls selfefficacy and depression. Self-efficacy for the maintenance of balance should be screened using the Falls Efficacy ScaleInternational,21 with scores greater than 24 indicating increased fall risk.13 Depression is associated with impaired mobility and increased falls incidence, and therefore screening for depression using the Geriatric Depression Scale-1522 (cut-off score >6)13 can be used to identify fall risk.

Screening
Physical therapists’ management of falls is predicated on
their ability to identify fall risk and movement dysfunction
as part of a multifactorial evaluation process to guide treatment choice. In 2017, through the Geriatrics Evidence
Database to Guide Effectiveness Initiative (GeriEDGE) task
force, Lusardi et al published a systematic review of history
questions, self-report measures, and performance-based
measures for assessing fall risk of community-dwelling
older adults.13 This CPG developed a screening process
using these results13 and the previous guidance statement
recommendations.12 The screening process includes medical

history questions, self-report measures, and performancebased functional measures as part of a multifactorial falls
screening13 (see Table 3). The GDG did not systematically
review the evidence for screening for falls risk, thus we
indicate the level of evidence for screening, but do not provide specific recommendations for falls risk screening.

The medical history questions, self-report measures, and
performance-based measures with the highest post-test
probability of identifying falls risk align with the Center
for Disease Control (CDC) “Stopping Elderly Accidents,
Death, and Injuries” (STEADI) processes20 and recent
guidelines on the management of falls.15 The details are
provided in the Falls Management Algorithm (Figure 1).

Screening may include self-report measures of falls selfefficacy and depression. Self-efficacy for the maintenance of
balance should be screened using the Falls Efficacy ScaleInternational,21 with scores greater than 24 indicating
increased fall risk.13 Depression is associated with impaired
mobility and increased falls incidence, and therefore screening for depression using the Geriatric Depression Scale-1522

(cut-off score >6)13 can be used to identify fall risk.

context_sources.text: Tests and measures that encompass body functions and structures, activity and participation, and environmental and personal factors should be performed during the examination. Based upon positive predictive values associated with fall risk established by the GeriEDGE SR we recommend the Timed Up and Go (TUG),23 5 times sit-tostand test,24 single limb stance with eyes open,25 the Berg Balance Scale (BBS)26 and self-selected gait speed.27 Scores greater than 11 seconds for the TUG and/or greater than 12 seconds on the 5 times sit-to-stand test indicate risk for falls.13 If the older adult is unable to maintain a single limb stance with eyes open greater than 6.5 seconds, fall risk is increased.13 A score of less than 50 on the BBS or a Self-selected walking speed less than 1.0 m/s indicate risk for falling.13 An intention of this CPG is to provide recommendations while considering the older adult’s level of fall risk. Determining the level of fall risk is part of the screening component of physical therapy management of older adults. Providing recommendations for fall risk classification is challenging due to inconsistent definitions in the literature, and variability in fall risk cut-off scores. As reinforced by Lusardi et al,13 the clinician can merge the findings of several tests to more accurately portray an older adult’s risk of falls. The Sherrington 2019 SR28 included studies that categorized higher risk as 1 or more falls and often some additional impairment on balance or mobility tests. The recent World CPG16 categorized high fall risk as those who had an injurious fall, 2 or more falls, a frailty diagnosis, inability to get up from the floor, or a loss of consciousness/suspected syncope. The GDG considers pre-fall loss of consciousness and syncope to be separate issues and out of the scope of this CPG. The GDG values a quantitative approach to assessing fall risk using change in post-test probability of validated questions, tests, and measures. We suggest that those who have a history of multiple or injurious falls, frailty, and/or are identified as having balance impairment by evidence-based tests, as suggested by Lusardi et al,13 should be classified as high risk.

context_sources.title: 2025 APTA-Geriatrics,Management of Fall Risk.pdf
context_sources.text: Examination After the screening process determines the level of fall risk, physical therapy management of people at risk for falls requires a thorough examination to identify movement related impairments and activity limitations. The examination leads to a movement system diagnosis that enables the development of a tailored intervention for falls management. Utilization of tests and measures with the best posttest probability for fall risk13 allows for the identification of who is at high risk of falls, but does not identify impairments in subdomains of balance, or other specific impairments (ie, in strength, balance, or cognition) that can guide what intervention is most appropriate for individuals. A recent study of the BESTest and MiniBESTest may support the relevance of these tests in this population.29 Magnani et al29 suggested age-standardized cut-off points for the BESTest and the Mini-BESTest. These tests may be particularly relevant to this population as they allow characterization of balance during standing and walking across multiple subdomains,29 and may better inform the evaluation and treatment planning process. Clinicians should refer to other evidence-based guidelines to assist with identification and classification of movement system impairments and limitations.30-32 A systematic review of examination strategies was outside the scope of this CPG. MULTIFACTORIAL MANAGEMENT PROGRAMS Multifactorial management programs include screening, assessment, referral to appropriate provider, and interventions within physical therapist scope of practice.12 Studies of fall prevention intervention programs that addressed multiple fall risk factors by providers from any discipline within and outside of PT practice in which a physical therapy provider might be involved were included. According to the ProFaNE Taxonomy, “multifactorial interventions are those interventions in which two or more sub-domains of intervention can be given to participants, and the interventions are linked to each individual’s risk profile, such that not all participants in a program receive the same combination of sub-domains.”1

The intensity of the resistance training interventions in studies included in 3 out of 4 of the systematic reviews used a resistance training intensity of exercise set at 60% to 80% of the 1 repetition maximum (1RM). The one other systematic review showed a majority of studies using 40% to 60% of 1RM. A majority of study participants exercised 2 to 3 days per week. The studies examined in the systematic reviews also tended to be longer in duration, with some studies lasting up to 6 months in duration. The mode of exercise varied widely from study to study within the separate systematic reviews. Modes included anything from traditional to wrist and ankle weights to hydraulic and pneumatic resistance. However, studies often just referred to progressive resistive exercise (PRE) and did not define a mode of exercise. In addition, bouts of exercise alternated between high intensity intervals and continuous bouts of 8 to 10 reps of a single exercise. With regard to selection of interventions, resistance training provides an alternate mode of exercise with expected clinical outcomes comparable to that of other interventions considered in the present CPG, although it should be noted that there are no meta-analyses and only a few individual trials of resistance versus aerobic exercise training.105–107 Clinical trials have only focused on the addition of resistance training to aerobic exercise, and is thus a separate key action statement. Resistance training can be especially effective in patients that do not tolerate continuous or interval aerobic training or other therapeutic modalities. Accommodating patient preference for mode of exercise may increase patient adherence, and thus resistance training should be offered as an option. that initially the physical therapist is conservative in addressing the progression of strength in patients with HF. Although Valsalva can occur with higher weight loads, evidence towards the negative effect of the Valsalva is weak and conscious cuing on the part of the physical therapist to avoid the Valsalva maneuver can increase the patient’s safety during the task. The increase in core stability using the Valsalva maneuver when lifting can also be accomplished, without increased atrial pressure, using forced exhalation during lifting.108 The clinician should also consider repetition to failure. If a patient is easily able to complete 10 reps of an exercise, reassessment of 1RM may be warranted.104 With regard to safety, no systematic review reported an increase in adverse events associated with resistance training. However, it is important to note that the patients studied met relatively strict inclusion criteria. Transient musculoskeletal pain was the most commonly reported complication among studies that was able to be resolved through adjustment of the exercises performed with few subsequent drop-outs.

The intensity of the resistance training interventions in
studies included in 3 out of 4 of the systematic reviews
used a resistance training intensity of exercise set at 60%
to 80% of the 1 repetition maximum (1RM). The one other
systematic review showed a majority of studies using 40%
to 60% of 1RM. A majority of study participants exercised

2 to 3 days per week. The studies examined in the
systematic reviews also tended to be longer in duration,
with some studies lasting up to 6 months in duration. The
mode of exercise varied widely from study to study within
the separate systematic reviews. Modes included anything
from traditional to wrist and ankle weights to hydraulic
and pneumatic resistance. However, studies often just
referred to progressive resistive exercise (PRE) and did
not define a mode of exercise. In addition, bouts of
exercise alternated between high intensity intervals and
continuous bouts of 8 to 10 reps of a single exercise.

With regard to selection of interventions, resistance
training provides an alternate mode of exercise with
expected clinical outcomes comparable to that of other
interventions considered in the present CPG, although it
should be noted that there are no meta-analyses and only
a few individual trials of resistance versus aerobic exercise
training.105–107 Clinical trials have only focused on the
addition of resistance training to aerobic exercise, and is
thus a separate key action statement. Resistance training
can be especially effective in patients that do not tolerate
continuous or interval aerobic training or other
therapeutic modalities. Accommodating patient preference
for mode of exercise may increase patient adherence, and
thus resistance training should be offered as
an option.

that initially the physical therapist is conservative in
addressing the progression of strength in patients with HF.

Although Valsalva can occur with higher weight loads,
evidence towards the negative effect of the Valsalva is
weak and conscious cuing on the part of the physical
therapist to avoid the Valsalva maneuver can increase the
patient’s safety during the task. The increase in core
stability using the Valsalva maneuver when lifting can also
be accomplished, without increased atrial pressure, using
forced exhalation during lifting.108 The clinician should
also consider repetition to failure. If a patient is easily
able to complete 10 reps of an exercise, reassessment of
1RM may be warranted.104

With regard to safety, no systematic review reported an
increase in adverse events associated with resistance
training. However, it is important to note that the patients
studied met relatively strict inclusion criteria. Transient
musculoskeletal pain was the most commonly reported
complication among studies that was able to be resolved
through adjustment of the exercises performed with few
subsequent drop-outs.

A single level I high-quality RCT reported no dif
ference in Kujala score or worst pain between
healthy adults with PFP who received 8 weeks of
standard knee exercise therapy (3 sets of 7 to 10 repetitions
at approximately 70% of 1-repetition maximum) and those
who received 8 weeks of blood flow restriction training plus
high-repetition knee exercise therapy (1 set of 30 repetitions
or volitional failure, followed by 3 sets of 15 repetitions, all at
30% of 1-repetition maximum).115 While a significantly great
er reduction in pain VAS score during ADLs was observed in
the blood flow restriction group compared with standard
knee-targeted exercise therapy, between-group differences on
the VAS did not exceed the MCID (20 mm).58 A subgroup
analysis revealed that those with painful resisted knee exten
sion experienced greater increases in quadriceps strength
with blood flow restriction therapy plus knee exercise therapy
than did those who received only standard knee exercise
therapy.

It is unclear whether strengthening leads to additional improvement of these outcomes in a multimodal treatment regimen due to conflicting results in the studies reviewed. For either isotonic or eccentric strengthening, the following dosing parameters were suggested: 3 sets of 15 repetitions for 6-12 weeks based on moderate evidence. No harms or adverse effects related to the exercise programs were reported.16

participate in multifactorial management programs addressing falls and fall risk for older adults. A multifactorial approach to fall risk management in older adults is supported by robust evidence (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong). A multicomponent exercise program that incorporates balance training and other modes of exercise, such as resistance training or Tai Chi, is strongly recommended for reducing the risk and rate of falls (Evidence Quality/ Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong). The guideline strongly recommends that balance training interventions be progressive and sufficiently challenging, involve limb and whole-body movements, changes in base of support, and reduced upper limb support (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong). Additionally, Tai Chi is strongly recommended for older adults in particular those at lower fall risk (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong). The guideline makes a strong recommendation for environmental assessments and necessary modifications for older adults at higher risk (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong). Providing or prescribing resistance training ALONE to reduce fall risk and rate is not recommended, as it offers limited benefits.(Evidence Quality/Level: II, Recommendation Strength: Moderate). This guideline also provides several weak recommendations. While reactive step (perturbation) training is a potential component of balance training, the evidence supporting this intervention is mixed (Evidence Quality/ Level: II, Recommendation Strength: Weak) in comparison to strong evidence for volitional step training or balance training. Additionally, this guideline recommends a comprehensive approach that combines tailored education with individualized exercise intervention, addressing identified risk factors, home hazards, strength and balance impairments, and referral to other providers when necessary, especially for factors outside the scope of physical therapy (Evidence Quality/Level: V, Recommendation Strength: Expert Opinion). The recommendation for this comprehensive approach is predicated upon expert opinion, but each individual component is recommended based upon robust evidence. These recommendations collectively guide physical therapists in adopting evidencebased practices to manage fall risk, while also highlighting the limitations and areas requiring further research.

effectiveness of balance training to reduce fall risk, providing resistance training ALONE is not sufficient. For people with identified impairments, it is the standard of practice to provide tailored, progressive resistance exercises to address these deficits within a multicomponent plan. Resistance exercise ALONE was not recommended due to the uncertainty of its effect on fall rate and risk. The studies that we reviewed had several limitations such as small sample sizes, no study stratified by their sample by risk of falls, and moderate-to-high risk of bias was present. The overwhelming majority of studies reported minimal adverse events from resistance training performed as part of a multicomponent exercise program, such as falls during exercise, pain during exercise, muscle soreness, muscle strain, low back pain, and abnormal heart rhythm. Evidence Synthesis Overall, the rate ratios are of low clinically meaningful value with insignificant confidence intervals. Estimates of risk and rate ratios are found in Table 11. Metaanalysis of acceptable or higher quality that found resistance training alone reported >1.0 fall rate ratio in two studies,14,28 no change in rate ratio in a study,75 and reduced rate ratio in one study.48 Fall risk ratio had similar findings with three of three studies reporting a ratio between 0.81 and 1.00 with insignificant confidence intervals.28,75,76 In one SR without metaanalysis,77 resistance training was viewed favorably concerning fall risk reduction when applied conventionally or as part of ADLs and when compared to usual care or relaxation training. Resistance training protocols employed differing doses and formats. Individual studies from the meta-analyses were further explored to identify specific characteristics for frequency, intensity, time, and types. Resistance exercise was often group-based, performed for 50-minute sessions, two-to-three times per week for 25 to 52 weeks.78-80 None of the studies demonstrated a decrease in fall rate or risk. The lack of change supports the recommendation that resistance training should not be performed in isolation, but as a component of a patient management plan as recommended in the multicomponent recommendation section. The safety of resistance training was further demonstrated in a recent meta-analysis of RCTs of long-term exercise interventions that found no difference between exercise and control groups in dropout due to health issues or mortality.68

Recommendation: Dosage, Intensity, and Components Physical therapists must prescribe exercise programs to older adults to be performed at least 150 minutes to 3 hours per week, lasting from 6 to 12 months, and must include progressive and sufficiently challenging balance training. (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Strength: Strong) Rationale Multicomponent exercise programs that include more than 150 minutes of exercise weekly are most effective in reducing fall rates48 and programs of 6 to 12 months duration are most effective in reducing fall rate and risk.60 Evidence from one meta-analysis61 examining the most effective combination of exercises in studies with longer follow-up times indicated that the most effective combination reduced risk by 35%, and included all categories of exercise combined, including gait, balance, and functional training, resistance training, flexibility exercises, and 3D training such as Tai Chi or dance. Evidence Synthesis Duration, intensity, and components of mixed singleand multi-component exercise programs In three separate SRs, Sherrington et al13,14,54 investigated the intensity, duration, and components of mixed singleand multi-component exercise interventions and found that the highest rate reductions were found with programs that included high intensity/high challenge balance training, did not include walking programs, had doses greater than 50 hours, and had frequencies greater than 3 hours per week. Differences in fall risk and rate reduction according to duration, intensity, or exercise components are summarized in Table 7. The most recent high-quality SR14 showed a 50% reduction in falls in programs that included more than 3 hours per week and balance and functional training.

response: Resistance exercise alone is not sufficient to prevent falls in older adults without balance training. The guideline explicitly states that resistance training ALONE is not recommended for reducing fall risk and rate, as it offers limited benefits [SOURCE 1]. Additionally, it is recommended that balance training interventions be progressive and sufficiently challenging, involving limb and whole-body movements, changes in base of support, and reduced upper limb support [SOURCE 1]. The guideline also emphasizes that a multicomponent exercise program incorporating balance training and other modes of exercise, such as resistance training or Tai Chi, is strongly recommended for reducing the risk and rate of falls [SOURCE 1].

those at lower fall risk (Evidence Quality/Level: I,

(Evidence Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength:
Strong). Providing or prescribing resistance training
ALONE to reduce fall risk and rate is not recommended,
as it offers limited benefits.(Evidence Quality/Level: II,
Recommendation Strength: Moderate).

This guideline also provides several weak recommendations. While reactive step (perturbation) training is
a potential component of balance training, the evidence
supporting this intervention is mixed (Evidence Quality/
Level: II, Recommendation Strength: Weak) in comparison to strong evidence for volitional step training or balance training. Additionally, this guideline recommends
a comprehensive approach that combines tailored education with individualized exercise intervention, addressing
identified risk factors, home hazards, strength and balance impairments, and referral to other providers when
necessary, especially for factors outside the scope of physical therapy (Evidence Quality/Level: V, Recommendation
Strength: Expert Opinion). The recommendation for this
comprehensive approach is predicated upon expert opinion, but each individual component is recommended
based upon robust evidence. These recommendations collectively guide physical therapists in adopting evidencebased practices to manage fall risk, while also highlighting
the limitations and areas requiring further research.

metadata.embedding_text:
effectiveness of balance training to reduce fall risk, providing resistance training ALONE is not sufficient. For
people with identified impairments, it is the standard of
practice to provide tailored, progressive resistance exercises to address these deficits within a multicomponent
plan.

Resistance exercise ALONE was not recommended due
to the uncertainty of its effect on fall rate and risk. The
studies that we reviewed had several limitations such as
small sample sizes, no study stratified by their sample by
risk of falls, and moderate-to-high risk of bias was present.
The overwhelming majority of studies reported minimal
adverse events from resistance training performed as part
of a multicomponent exercise program, such as falls during
exercise, pain during exercise, muscle soreness, muscle
strain, low back pain, and abnormal heart rhythm.

Evidence Synthesis
Overall, the rate ratios are of low clinically meaningful
value with insignificant confidence intervals. Estimates
of risk and rate ratios are found in Table 11. Metaanalysis of acceptable or higher quality that found resistance training alone reported >1.0 fall rate ratio in two
studies,14,28 no change in rate ratio in a study,75 and
reduced rate ratio in one study.48 Fall risk ratio had
similar findings with three of three studies reporting
a ratio between 0.81 and 1.00 with insignificant confidence intervals.28,75,76 In one SR without metaanalysis,77 resistance training was viewed favorably
concerning fall risk reduction when applied conventionally or as part of ADLs and when compared to usual care
or relaxation training.

Resistance training protocols employed differing doses
and formats. Individual studies from the meta-analyses
were further explored to identify specific characteristics
for frequency, intensity, time, and types. Resistance exercise
was often group-based, performed for 50-minute sessions,
two-to-three times per week for 25 to 52 weeks.78-80 None
of the studies demonstrated a decrease in fall rate or risk.
The lack of change supports the recommendation that
resistance training should not be performed in isolation,
but as a component of a patient management plan as recommended in the multicomponent recommendation section.

The safety of resistance training was further demonstrated in a recent meta-analysis of RCTs of long-term
exercise interventions that found no difference between
exercise and control groups in dropout due to health
issues or mortality.68

These recommendations collectively guide physical therapists in adopting evidencebased practices to manage fall risk, while also highlighting the limitations and areas requiring further research.

Resistance exercise ALONE was not recommended due to the uncertainty of its effect on fall rate and risk. The studies that we reviewed had several limitations such as small sample sizes, no study stratified by their sample by risk of falls, and moderate-to-high risk of bias was present. The overwhelming majority of studies reported minimal adverse events from resistance training performed as part of a multicomponent exercise program, such as falls during exercise, pain during exercise, muscle soreness, muscle strain, low back pain, and abnormal heart rhythm. As people with diabetes who are at risk of foot ulceration will likely not be aware of appropriate exercises, we recommend them to undergo a foot assessment and exercise prescription by an adequately trained healthcare professional prior to commencing exercise. Weekly evaluation of progress with training and modification of the program in collaboration with the professional is recommended. While this involves moderate costs, we assessed the importance of involving a healthcare professional for supervision and support as being of value because of the nature of the intervention, and also found better results on some outcomes if supervision was incorporated. People with a pre-ulcerative lesion or with a foot ulcer should not partake in foot-related exercises in which the foot is mechanically loaded, as there is still no evidence if these exercises are safe. Advising people with diabetes at low to moderate risk of foot ulceration (IWGDF risk 1 or 2) to perform foot-related exercises is based on low certainty of evidence (8). Any potential for harm is outweighed by both general health benefits of exercise and specific improvements to the complex musculoskeletal deficits that develop with diabetes. Foot-related exercises are relatively easy to perform autonomously, are acceptable to people with diabetes, and feasible to execute. Minimal exercise equipment is required, for example elastic bands or exercise balls. As adherence may be a challenge, we advise health practitioners to continue to motivate people with diabetes to complete the exercise program as prescribed. We recommend regularly evaluating the training and outcome progress and updating the program when required. However, lifelong continued support from a health trained professional is not feasible. We therefore recommend that people with diabetes continue after the program, without professional support, preferably with the support of booklets, videos or rehabilitation technology tools. Feasibility of this part of our recommendation has not been studied, and it is unknown how people with diabetes assess such continuation. Because we expect the positive outcomes of the programs to continue if the exercises are continued, we do recommend people with diabetes to keep performing the exercise after the 8-12 weeks program.
[/SOURCE 1]

Recommendation 13: Consider communicating to a person with diabetes who is at low or moderate risk for foot ulceration (IWGDF risk 1 or 2) that an increase in the level of walking-related weightbearing daily activity by an extra 1000 steps/day is likely to be safe regarding risk of foot ulceration. Advise this person to wear appropriate footwear when undertaking weight-bearing activities, and to frequently monitor the skin for (pre-)ulcerative lesions. (Conditional; Low) Rationale: Exercise has general health benefits for people with diabetes, including specific improvements to the complex musculoskeletal deficits that develop with diabetes (57). However, when this exercise is weight-bearing, it increases the cumulative plantar tissue stress on the foot and should therefore be considered in the context of foot disease (58). Based on 4 studies where people with diabetes at risk of foot ulceration participated in a training program that increased their weight-bearing activity but where this did not result in increased incidence of ulceration (8), we suggest to consider advising people at low or moderate risk for ulceration (IWGDF 1 or 2) that a gradual increase in the level of walking-related weight-bearing activity is likely to be safe. We define an increase as a gradual increase in activity with an end goal of an additional 1000 steps/day, based on the increases seen in these 4 studies (8), and an RCT that showed such an increase to be beneficial for glycaemic control in people with diabetes (59). It is advisable to avoid sudden spikes in activity and to increase daily steps by a maximum of 10% per week, until a person reaches an overall increase of 1000 steps/day in comparison to baseline. This increase in daily steps may also be considered for those people with IWGDF risk 3 (60), as evidence showed that these people take on average the same number of daily steps compared to those at low or moderate risk (61). Thus it is probably safe, especially if they wear appropriate footwear when performing weightbearing activities (see recommendations 8-11).
[/SOURCE 2]

Recommendation 12: Consider advising and referring a person with diabetes who is at low or moderate risk for foot ulceration (IWGDF risk 1 or 2) to participate in an 8-12-weeks foot-ankle exercise program, preferably under the supervision of an appropriately trained healthcare professional, and to continue performing foot-ankle exercises afterwards, with the aim of reducing risk factors of ulceration. (Conditional; Low) Rationale: The risk of ulceration increases in the presence of risk factors. Interventions described in this guideline as part of education (section 3) and footwear (section 4) may help prevent foot ulcers, but do not mitigate the risk factors underlying them. While not all risk factors can be modified, some can. This includes plantar pressure distribution, neuropathy signs and symptoms, deficits in foot sensation, footankle joint mobility and strength (8). Various forms of foot-related exercises are possible when aiming to improve these modifiable risk factors for foot ulceration. These exercises can include stretching and strengthening of the foot and ankle joints and musculature and functional exercises, such as balance and gait exercises (8). These exercises are generally provided in 8-12 weeks training programs, supervised by physical therapists or other qualified and trained professionals, face-to-face or home-based, individually or in groups. In our meta-analyses, we found that these exercise programs do not increase the risk of ulceration, while improving foot and ankle joint range of motion, neuropathy signs and symptoms and plantar pressure distribution (8). As such, the desirable effects outweigh the undesirable effects.
[/SOURCE 4]

We recommend screening a person with diabetes at very low risk for foot ulceration annually for loss of protective sensation and peripheral artery disease, and screening persons at higher risk at higher frequencies for additional risk factors. For preventing a foot ulcer, educate persons at-risk about appropriate foot self-care, educate not to walk without suitable foot protection, and treat any preulcerative lesion on the foot. Educate moderate-to-high risk people with diabetes to wear properly fitting, accommodative, therapeutic footwear, and consider coaching them to monitor foot skin temperature. Prescribe therapeutic footwear that has a demonstrated plantar pressure relieving effect during walking, to help prevent plantar foot ulcer recurrence. Consider advising people at low-tomoderate risk to undertake a, preferably supervised, foot-ankle exercise program to reduce ulcer risk factors, and consider communicating that a total increase in weight-bearing activity of 1000 steps/day is likely safe with regards to risk of ulceration. In people with non-rigid hammertoe with pre-ulcerative lesion, consider flexor tendon tenotomy. We suggest not to use a nerve decompression procedure to help prevent foot ulcers. Provide integrated foot care for moderate-to-high-risk people with diabetes to help prevent (recurrence of) ulceration.
[/SOURCE 5]

metadata.embedding_text:
Recommendation 12: Consider advising and referring a person with diabetes who is at low or moderate
risk for foot ulceration (IWGDF risk 1 or 2) to participate in an 8-12-weeks foot-ankle exercise
program, preferably under the supervision of an appropriately trained healthcare professional, and to
continue performing foot-ankle exercises afterwards, with the aim of reducing risk factors of ulceration.
(Conditional; Low) Rationale: The risk of ulceration increases in the presence of risk factors. Interventions described in this
guideline as part of education (section 3) and footwear (section 4) may help prevent foot ulcers, but do
not mitigate the risk factors underlying them. While not all risk factors can be modified, some can. This
includes plantar pressure distribution, neuropathy signs and symptoms, deficits in foot sensation, footankle joint mobility and strength (8). Various forms of foot-related exercises are possible when aiming to
improve these modifiable risk factors for foot ulceration. These exercises can include stretching and
strengthening of the foot and ankle joints and musculature and functional exercises, such as balance and
gait exercises (8). These exercises are generally provided in 8-12 weeks training programs, supervised by
physical therapists or other qualified and trained professionals, face-to-face or home-based, individually
or in groups. In our meta-analyses, we found that these exercise programs do not increase the risk of
ulceration, while improving foot and ankle joint range of motion, neuropathy signs and symptoms and
plantar pressure distribution (8). As such, the desirable effects outweigh the undesirable effects.

metadata.organization: International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot
metadata.embedding_text:
We recommend screening a person with diabetes at very low risk for foot ulceration annually for loss of
protective sensation and peripheral artery disease, and screening persons at higher risk at higher
frequencies for additional risk factors. For preventing a foot ulcer, educate persons at-risk about
appropriate foot self-care, educate not to walk without suitable foot protection, and treat any preulcerative lesion on the foot. Educate moderate-to-high risk people with diabetes to wear properly
fitting, accommodative, therapeutic footwear, and consider coaching them to monitor foot skin
temperature. Prescribe therapeutic footwear that has a demonstrated plantar pressure relieving effect
during walking, to help prevent plantar foot ulcer recurrence. Consider advising people at low-tomoderate risk to undertake a, preferably supervised, foot-ankle exercise program to reduce ulcer risk
factors, and consider communicating that a total increase in weight-bearing activity of 1000 steps/day is
likely safe with regards to risk of ulceration. In people with non-rigid hammertoe with pre-ulcerative
lesion, consider flexor tendon tenotomy. We suggest not to use a nerve decompression procedure to
help prevent foot ulcers. Provide integrated foot care for moderate-to-high-risk people with diabetes to
help prevent (recurrence of) ulceration.

context_sources.text: As people with diabetes who are at risk of foot ulceration will likely not be aware of appropriate exercises, we recommend them to undergo a foot assessment and exercise prescription by an adequately trained healthcare professional prior to commencing exercise. Weekly evaluation of progress with training and modification of the program in collaboration with the professional is recommended. While this involves moderate costs, we assessed the importance of involving a healthcare professional for supervision and support as being of value because of the nature of the intervention, and also found better results on some outcomes if supervision was incorporated. People with a pre-ulcerative lesion or with a foot ulcer should not partake in foot-related exercises in which the foot is mechanically loaded, as there is still no evidence if these exercises are safe. Advising people with diabetes at low to moderate risk of foot ulceration (IWGDF risk 1 or 2) to perform foot-related exercises is based on low certainty of evidence (8). Any potential for harm is outweighed by both general health benefits of exercise and specific improvements to the complex musculoskeletal deficits that develop with diabetes. Foot-related exercises are relatively easy to perform autonomously, are acceptable to people with diabetes, and feasible to execute. Minimal exercise equipment is required, for example elastic bands or exercise balls. As adherence may be a challenge, we advise health practitioners to continue to motivate people with diabetes to complete the exercise program as prescribed. We recommend regularly evaluating the training and outcome progress and updating the program when required. However, lifelong continued support from a health trained professional is not feasible. We therefore recommend that people with diabetes continue after the program, without professional support, preferably with the support of booklets, videos or rehabilitation technology tools. Feasibility of this part of our recommendation has not been studied, and it is unknown how people with diabetes assess such continuation. Because we expect the positive outcomes of the programs to continue if the exercises are continued, we do recommend people with diabetes to keep performing the exercise after the 8-12 weeks program.

context_sources.text: Recommendation 13: Consider communicating to a person with diabetes who is at low or moderate risk for foot ulceration (IWGDF risk 1 or 2) that an increase in the level of walking-related weightbearing daily activity by an extra 1000 steps/day is likely to be safe regarding risk of foot ulceration. Advise this person to wear appropriate footwear when undertaking weight-bearing activities, and to frequently monitor the skin for (pre-)ulcerative lesions. (Conditional; Low) Rationale: Exercise has general health benefits for people with diabetes, including specific improvements to the complex musculoskeletal deficits that develop with diabetes (57). However, when this exercise is weight-bearing, it increases the cumulative plantar tissue stress on the foot and should therefore be considered in the context of foot disease (58). Based on 4 studies where people with diabetes at risk of foot ulceration participated in a training program that increased their weight-bearing activity but where this did not result in increased incidence of ulceration (8), we suggest to consider advising people at low or moderate risk for ulceration (IWGDF 1 or 2) that a gradual increase in the level of walking-related weight-bearing activity is likely to be safe. We define an increase as a gradual increase in activity with an end goal of an additional 1000 steps/day, based on the increases seen in these 4 studies (8), and an RCT that showed such an increase to be beneficial for glycaemic control in people with diabetes (59). It is advisable to avoid sudden spikes in activity and to increase daily steps by a maximum of 10% per week, until a person reaches an overall increase of 1000 steps/day in comparison to baseline. This increase in daily steps may also be considered for those people with IWGDF risk 3 (60), as evidence showed that these people take on average the same number of daily steps compared to those at low or moderate risk (61). Thus it is probably safe, especially if they wear appropriate footwear when performing weightbearing activities (see recommendations 8-11).
